specPoints.text: describe an experiment to prepare a pure, dry sample of a soluble salt, starting from an acid and alkali

primer.text: From Acid-Alkali Titrations you already know how a burette and a pipette measure reacting volumes exactly. This note borrows that skill for making a dry salt sample from an acid and an alkali, where the indicator does its job once and is then left out.

lessons.title: Preparation of a soluble salt using a titration
sourceHeadings: Preparation of a soluble salt using a titration
lessons.opening: When both starting materials are soluble, the salt is prepared from an acid and an alkali, and a titration shows exactly when they have reacted in the right proportions. A few drops of indicator reveal the neutral point during the measured run. Because the indicator would contaminate the product, the real batch repeats the found volumes with no indicator present.
keyPoints: A dry salt can be prepared from an acid and an alkali.
A pipette measures the alkali into a conical flask.
A few drops of indicator such as phenolphthalein or methyl orange are added.
The acid is run in slowly from a burette until the indicator just changes colour.
The starting and final burette readings give the volume of acid added.

low.restatement: Measure the alkali into a flask with a pipette, add indicator drops, then run acid in from a burette until the colour just changes. Read the burette before and after to find the volume that reacted.
low.analogy: The indicator is like a referee with a flag: it cannot play in the real match, but it tells you exactly when the winning point was scored.
low.examPointer: Name the apparatus with its role, pipette for the alkali and burette for the acid, because mixed-up apparatus lists cost method marks.

medium.restatement: The titration finds the exact reacting ratio rather than preparing the product itself. Once the acid volume that neutralises the alkali is known, that pair of volumes can be repeated cleanly, because reacting in the found ratio leaves neither acid nor alkali behind in the salt solution.
medium.analogy: It is like test-driving a recipe in a small pan before cooking the full pot: the trial tells you the exact quantities, and the real batch follows them without the tester's tasting spoon in it.
medium.examPointer: If asked why the trial matters, say it fixes the exact volume ratio so the clean batch has no leftover acid or alkali to contaminate the crystals.

check.stem: Why can the method of adding insoluble base in excess not be used here?

options.text: Because both reactants are soluble, so no excess solid could be filtered off
options.explanation: With an alkali there is no undissolved solid to remove, so the excess-and-filter trick has nothing to work on.

options.text: Because acids cannot react with alkalis
options.explanation: Acids and alkalis neutralise each other readily; that is the reaction being used.

options.text: Because alkalis are too dangerous to handle
options.explanation: Dilute alkalis are handled routinely in titrations with normal care.

options.text: Because the salt formed would be insoluble
options.explanation: The salt from an acid and alkali is soluble by design of this method.

check.stem: Which pieces of apparatus measure the two reactants?

options.text: A pipette for the alkali and a burette for the acid
options.explanation: That is the standard allocation in the source method.

options.text: A burette for the alkali and a pipette for the acid
options.explanation: The roles can be swapped in principle, but the method of record puts the alkali in the flask by pipette and the acid in the burette.

options.text: A measuring cylinder for both
options.explanation: A cylinder is too imprecise for the exact ratio this preparation needs.

options.text: A conical flask for both
options.explanation: The flask holds the reaction; it does not measure anything.

check.stem: What is the purpose of the indicator in the first run?

options.text: To show when the acid and alkali have exactly reacted
options.explanation: The colour change marks the neutral point of the titration.

options.text: To colour the final crystals
options.explanation: The indicator is deliberately absent from the real batch, so it colours nothing.

options.text: To speed up the reaction
options.explanation: Indicators do not change reaction speeds; they report pH.

options.text: To keep the solution alkaline
options.explanation: The indicator is a reporter, not a reactant, and keeps nothing alkaline.

check.stem: Name an indicator suitable for this titration.

options.text: Phenolphthalein
options.explanation: The source names phenolphthalein or methyl orange as the choices.

options.text: Anhydrous copper(II) sulfate
options.explanation: That powder tests for water; it is not an acid-alkali indicator.

options.text: Sodium hydroxide solution
options.explanation: Sodium hydroxide is the alkali reactant itself, not an indicator.

options.text: Limewater
options.explanation: Limewater is the carbon dioxide test reagent, not an indicator here.

check.stem: How is the volume of acid added found from the burette readings?

options.text: Final reading minus initial reading
options.explanation: The difference between the two readings is the delivered volume.

options.text: Initial reading minus final reading
options.explanation: That gives a negative number, since the burette reading falls as liquid leaves.

options.text: The two readings added together
options.explanation: Adding readings double-counts the liquid instead of finding the difference.

options.text: The final reading halved
options.explanation: Nothing in the method involves halving; the difference is what matters.

lessons.title: Method
lessons.opening: Once the neutral volume is known, the same volumes of acid and alkali are mixed again with the indicator left out, so nothing but salt and water is made. The solution is heated until part of the water has gone, leaving a saturated solution. Crystals are then allowed to form, the liquid above them is poured off, and the solid is left to dry.
keyPoints: The measured volumes are repeated without the indicator.
Heating partially evaporates the solution, leaving a saturated solution.
Crystals are left to form, then the excess solution is decanted off.
Some water is deliberately left behind in the crystals.
Leaving water behind allows for water of crystallisation and stops the salt overheating and decomposing.

low.restatement: Repeat the titration volumes with no indicator, then heat the solution until it is saturated but not dry. Let crystals form, pour off the surplus liquid and let the solid dry in air.
low.analogy: Stopping the heating with water left is like taking bread out before it burns: a little moisture is wanted, and pushing all the way to dryness spoils the product.
low.examPointer: Evaporate to saturated, never to dryness, and give both reasons if asked: water of crystallisation and avoiding decomposition.

medium.restatement: The clean repeat guarantees the crystals grow from pure salt solution with no dye trapped inside. Partial evaporation leaves the solution saturated, so on cooling and standing the salt crystallises with its waters of crystallisation intact, and any mother liquor holding impurities is decanted away rather than cooked onto the solid.
medium.analogy: Decanting the leftover liquid is like draining the cooking water from pasta: what you want stays behind in the pot, and the flavoured water you throw away carries off what you do not.
medium.examPointer: Two-mark evaporation questions usually want the saturated-solution state plus the water-of-crystallisation reason, so quote both rather than one.

check.stem: Why is the second mixture made without indicator?

options.text: So the salt is not contaminated with indicator dye
options.explanation: Any indicator left in would colour the product and count as an impurity.

options.text: Because the indicator stops crystals forming
options.explanation: Indicators do not block crystallisation; the reason is purity, not mechanics.

options.text: Because the indicator is expensive
options.explanation: Costs are irrelevant; only a few drops are used anyway.

options.text: So the volumes can be measured again
options.explanation: The volumes are already known from the first run.

check.stem: What state is the solution in when heating stops?

options.text: Saturated, with some water still present
options.explanation: Heating stops at the saturated stage so crystals can form on standing.

options.text: Completely dry, with all water gone
options.explanation: Heating to dryness would overheat the salt and spoil the water of crystallisation.

options.text: Still dilute, with all the original water
options.explanation: No crystals could form from a solution that never concentrated.

options.text: Frozen, because crystals need cold
options.explanation: Crystals grow from solution on cooling, not from a frozen block.

check.stem: Why must some water remain when heating stops?

options.text: Some salts need water of crystallisation, and full dryness risks decomposition
options.explanation: Both halves are the source's stated reasons for the partial evaporation.

options.text: Water makes the crystals heavier to sell
options.explanation: Commercial reasoning plays no part in the chemistry.

options.text: Water is needed to dissolve the burette
options.explanation: The burette is not part of the crystallisation stage at all.

options.text: Dry salts are always dangerous
options.explanation: Dryness is not itself a hazard here; decomposition is the stated risk.

check.stem: What is done after crystallisation to isolate the solid?

options.text: The excess solution is decanted and the crystals left to dry
options.explanation: That is the closing sequence of the method of record.

options.text: The crystals are redissolved in fresh acid
options.explanation: Redissolving would restart the preparation instead of finishing it.

options.text: The crystals are heated until they melt
options.explanation: Melting would decompose the salt rather than purify it.

options.text: The crystals are washed in indicator
options.explanation: Indicator was deliberately excluded and must not return.

check.stem: Which method does this whole preparation rely on?

options.text: Titration between an acid and an alkali
options.explanation: The measured reacting volumes come from the titration technique.

options.text: Filtration of an insoluble base
options.explanation: No insoluble solid exists in this method to filter.

options.text: Precipitation from two soluble salts
options.explanation: That is the insoluble-salt preparation, a different method.

options.text: Heating a metal with sulfur directly
options.explanation: No direct element-plus-element synthesis appears here.

glossary.definition: A technique in which one solution is added to another from a burette until they exactly react.
A long graduated tube with a tap, used to deliver measured volumes of solution.
A calibrated tube used to transfer one fixed, accurate volume of liquid.
A dye whose colour changes to show the pH of a solution, marking the neutral point here.
A solution holding as much dissolved salt as it can at that temperature.
Water molecules built into a salt's crystal structure, written after a dot in its formula.
The change from liquid to vapour that concentrates a solution as it is heated.
The formation of ordered solid crystals as a concentrated solution loses water.

workedExample.prompt: A student prepares a pure, dry sample of sodium chloride from hydrochloric acid and sodium hydroxide solution. a) Name the apparatus used to measure each reactant. b) Why is indicator added in the first run but left out of the second? c) Why is the solution heated only until part of the water has evaporated, not to dryness?
steps: a) A pipette measures a fixed volume of the alkali into a conical flask; the acid is run in from a burette until the indicator just changes colour.
b) The indicator marks the neutral point so the exact reacting volumes are found; it would contaminate the salt, so the same volumes are mixed again with no indicator.
c) Heating stops once a saturated solution forms: leaving some water allows for water of crystallisation and prevents the salt from overheating and decomposing.
workedExample.finalAnswer: a) Pipette for the alkali, burette for the acid. b) The indicator finds the neutral point but would contaminate the product. c) To allow water of crystallisation and avoid decomposition.
